pos: n. & adj. (a worshipper of false gods; heathen)
etymology: Latin paganus, a countryman, from pagus, a village. Webster (1828) explains that the word “was originally applied to the inhabitants of the country, who on the first propagation of the christian religion adhered to the worship of false gods, or refused to receive christianity, after it had been received by the inhabitants of the cities.”
biblical_def: A pagan is one who worships false gods. Webster (1828) gives the sense in a row of plain synonyms: “A heathen; a Gentile; an idolater; one who worships false gods.” The word itself is not in the Authorized Version, which says heathen and Gentiles, but the condition is described exactly. Paul reminds the Corinthians, “Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led” (1Co 12:2), and the Ephesians that they were once “without Christ ... having no hope, and without God in the world” (Eph 2:12). The pagan is not a man without religion; he is a man whose worship has gone to the wrong place. Conversion is therefore a turning: the Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1Th 1:9). God has borne with the ignorance of the nations, “but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PAGAN, a heathen; a Gentile; an idolater; one who worships false gods. Adjective: heathenish; pertaining to the worship of false gods.
webster_full: PA'GAN, noun [Latin paganus, a peasant or countryman, from pagus, a village.]

A heathen; a Gentile; an idolater; one who worships false gods. This word was originally applied to the inhabitants of the country, who on the first propagation of the christian religion adhered to the worship of false gods, or refused to receive christianity, after it had been received by the inhabitants of the cities.
Heathen; heathenish; Gentile; noting a person who worships false gods.
1. Pertaining to the worship of false gods.
scriptures: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.
Eph 2:12
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
corruption_summary: Neo-paganism wears the name as a badge, recasting the worship of creation as nature-reverence and ancestral heritage; Scripture calls it being carried away unto dumb idols.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern revival of paganism presents itself as gentle: reverence for the earth, the seasons and the old gods of one's ancestors. Webster's definition strips the costume away. A pagan is one who worships false gods, and Paul describes that life not as freedom but as being “carried away” (1Co 12:2).

The opposite error treats the pagan as beyond reach, or as an enemy rather than a man to be called. The Thessalonians were pagans until they “turned to God from idols” (1Th 1:9). The word marks where a man stands, not where God must leave him.
roots_summary: Latin paganus, villager, from pagus, village: the countryman who held to the old gods after the cities received the gospel.
roots_lines: Latin pagus, a village or rural district.
Latin paganus, a countryman.
Webster (1828): applied to those in the country who adhered to false gods after the cities received Christianity.
The AV says heathen and Gentiles for the same condition.
Turned to God from idols (1Th 1:9).
usage: carried away unto these dumb idols (1Co 12:2)
turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God

pos: n. (self-imposed or imposed suffering for sin)
etymology: Old French penance, from Latin paenitentia, repentance. Webster (1828) enters PEN’ANCE with two senses: suffering undergone for one's faults, and, secondly, “Repentance.”
biblical_def: Penance in its first and common sense is suffering taken on to answer for sin. Webster (1828) defines it as “the suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority as a punishment for his faults, or as an expression of penitence; such as fasting, flagellation, wearing chains, etc.” and notes that it “is one of the seven sacraments of the Romish church.” His second sense is simply “Repentance.” Scripture keeps the two apart. Repentance is commanded of all men (Act 17:30); penance as satisfaction for sin is nowhere commanded, because the satisfaction is already made: “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). What God asks is not the pain of the body but the breaking of the heart: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psa 51:17); “rend your heart, and not your garments” (Joe 2:13). True repentance bears fruit, “works meet for repentance” (Act 26:20), but the fruit is the evidence of a turned heart, never the price of pardon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PENANCE, suffering voluntarily undergone or imposed as punishment for faults or as an expression of penitence; one of the seven sacraments of the Romish church. 2. Repentance.
webster_full: 1. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority as a punishment for his faults, or as an expression of penitence; such as fasting, flagellation, wearing chains, etc. penance is one of the seven sacraments of the Romish church.
scriptures: For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Joe 2:13
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
But shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance.
Mic 6:7
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
corruption_summary: Rome made penance a sacrament and a payment toward the temporal debt of sin; the popular mind keeps the same instinct, that a man must suffer enough before God will forgive.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman system turns repentance into a transaction: confession to a priest, absolution, and works of satisfaction imposed to pay what sin still owes. Webster records it plainly as “one of the seven sacraments of the Romish church.” Scripture knows two sacraments, not seven, and it knows one satisfaction, the “one offering” by which Christ “hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). Every added payment implies that offering was not enough.

The same instinct survives without a priest. A man punishes himself, withholds comfort from himself, or waits until he has felt bad long enough before he dares to pray. Micah answered it: “shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?” (Mic 6:7). God does not sell pardon for pain. He gives it freely to the broken and contrite heart (Psa 51:17).
roots_summary: Latin paenitentia, repentance, through Old French penance: a word that began as repentance and came to mean self-punishment for sin.
roots_lines: Latin paenitentia, repentance, regret.
Old French penance.
Webster (1828) sense 1: suffering undergone as punishment for faults.
Webster sense 2: repentance.
By one offering he hath perfected for ever (Heb 10:14).
usage: one of the seven sacraments of the Romish church
rend your heart, and not your garments (Joe 2:13)

pos: n. (one who keeps the forms of religion without its life)
etymology: English form, from Latin forma, with the agent suffix -ist. Webster (1828) enters FORM’ALIST with two senses.
biblical_def: A formalist keeps the outward forms of religion. Webster (1828) gives a neutral sense, “One who observes forms, or practices external ceremonies,” and then the sense the word more often bears: “One who regards appearances only, or observes the forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit of religion; a hypocrite.” He adds a sentence that could stand as a sermon: “A grave face and the regular practice of ceremonies have often gained to a formalist the reputation of piety.” Scripture describes the formalist in the last days as “Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away” (2Ti 3:5). Christ found him in the temple: “This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me” (Mat 15:8), and compared him to “whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones” (Mat 23:27). The forms God gave are good; the formalist's sin is to rest in them, to have the ordinance and not the Lord of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORMALIST, one who observes forms or external ceremonies; more generally, one who regards appearances only, keeping the forms of worship without the life and spirit of religion; a hypocrite.
webster_full: 1. One who observes forms, or practices external ceremonies.

More generally, 2. One who regards appearances only, or observes the forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit of religion; a hypocrite. A grave face and the regular practice of ceremonies have often gained to a formalist the reputation of piety.
scriptures: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
Mat 15:8
This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
Mat 6:16
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
corruption_summary: The charge of formalism is now aimed at order itself, so that liturgy, catechism and set worship are called dead and the absence of form is called life.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's formalist is the man who has the form without the life. The modern complaint moves the fault from the man to the form, as though a written prayer, a confession or an ordered service were the disease. Scripture does not condemn the form of godliness; it condemns “denying the power thereof” (2Ti 3:5). A church without forms can be as dead as one with them.

The opposite danger is the one Webster names: “A grave face and the regular practice of ceremonies have often gained to a formalist the reputation of piety.” Attendance, observance and a serious manner can be kept for years by a heart that is “far from me” (Mat 15:8). The cure is not to drop the forms but to come through them to Christ.
roots_summary: Latin forma, shape or appearance, plus -ist: one devoted to the outward shape of religion.
roots_lines: Latin forma, form, shape, appearance.
English agent suffix -ist.
Webster (1828) sense 1: one who observes forms or external ceremonies.
Webster sense 2: one who regards appearances only; a hypocrite.
A form of godliness, but denying the power thereof (2Ti 3:5).
usage: the forms of worship without the life and spirit of religion
a grave face and the regular practice of ceremonies
having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof

etymology: Greek presbyteros, elder, the comparative of presbys, old. Webster (1828) enters PRES’BYTER, “[Gr. old, elder.]” The English word priest descends from the same Greek word by way of Latin presbyter.
biblical_def: A presbyter is an elder of the church. Webster (1828) gives the primitive sense first: “In the primitive christian church, an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who had authority in the church, and whose duty was to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made him overseer.” That last clause is Paul’s own charge to the Ephesian elders: “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). The same men are called elders in Act 20:17 and overseers in Act 20:28, so the New Testament presbyter and bishop are one office. The apostles ordained “elders in every church” (Act 14:23), and Titus was left in Crete to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Peter, an apostle, calls himself “also an elder” and charges his fellow presbyters, “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof” (1Pe 5:1-2). Some labour “in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17); all are shepherds under the chief Shepherd, not priests offering sacrifice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PRESBYTER, in the primitive church an elder with authority, whose duty was to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit made him overseer; 2. a priest with pastoral charge of a congregation; 3. a presbyterian.
webster_full: 1. In the primitive christian church, an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who had authority in the church, and whose duty was to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made him overseer.
2. A priest; a person who has the pastoral charge of a particular church and congregation; called in the Saxon laws, mass-priest.
scriptures: And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed:
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: The elder of the New Testament became, in later usage, a sacrificing priest; Webster's own sense 2 and the Saxon mass-priest show how far the word was carried from the shepherd Paul charged at Miletus.
corruption_paragraphs: The word presbyter, elder, is the parent of the English word priest, and history explains the drift. As the Lord's Supper was turned into a sacrifice, the elder who served it was turned into a priest who offered it; Webster records the end of that road in the Saxon term “mass-priest.” The New Testament elder offers no sacrifice. Christ's one offering is finished, and the presbyter's work is to feed the flock with the word (Act 20:28; 1Ti 5:17).

The opposite corruption empties the office. Where elders are chosen as a board of directors, or not at all, the flock is left without the oversight Peter commanded (1Pe 5:2). The apostles ordained elders “in every church” (Act 14:23); the office is not optional, and it is held by qualified men who rule and shepherd under Christ.
roots_summary: Greek presbyteros, elder, from presbys, old: the overseer and shepherd of a local church; the root of English priest.
roots_lines: Greek presbys, old; presbyteros, older, elder.
Latin presbyter, borrowed from the Greek.
English priest descends from the same word.
Webster (1828) sense 1: in the primitive church, an elder who fed the flock.
Elders (Act 20:17) are called overseers (Act 20:28).
usage: to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made him overseer
the same office as bishop in the New Testament
